claims.text: HEA nanoparticle premelting and melting behavior is primarily governed by configurational entropy.
Configurational entropy suppresses surface diffusion and atomic mobility in HEA nanoparticles.
Suppressed atomic mobility stabilizes the solid phase and elevates melting temperature relative to low-entropy or pure-element nanoparticles.
Atomic-scale configurational entropy manifests as random mixing and local chemical disorder.
Random mixing and local chemical disorder affect surface and bulk atomic mobility.
High configurational entropy disrupts coordinated atomic motion and reduces surface diffusion rates.
Reduced surface diffusion delays the onset of premelting and raises melting temperature.
The proposed entropy effect is most pronounced at the nanoscale because surface effects dominate.
HEA nanoparticles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than same-size pure-element or binary-alloy nanoparticles.
HEA nanoparticles will have a higher melting point than same-size pure-element or binary-alloy nanoparticles.
The melting or premelting temperature difference will exceed approximately 10–50 K.
The thermal-stability difference will scale with compositional complexity.
The hypothesis is proposed to hold for well-mixed HEA nanoparticles containing at least five elements and measuring 5–20 nm.
The hypothesis may not apply to particles larger than 50 nm.
Poor mixing, surface segregation, or phase separation may weaken or invalidate the proposed effect.
The quantitative melting-point elevation depends on mixing, particle size, and surface cleanliness.
HEA, pure-element, and binary-alloy nanoparticles should be compared at matched size, morphology, surface cleanliness, atmosphere, and heating conditions.
Premelting onset, complete liquefaction temperature, surface diffusion, and morphology should be measured during heating.
A premelting or melting elevation below 5 K, or no elevation, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes low-entropy or pure-element particles of similar composition, but a pure Ni control cannot have a composition similar to CoCrFeMnNi. The proposed comparison therefore changes elemental identity and associated thermodynamic properties along with configurational complexity, so it does not isolate the stated governing factor.
The predicted elevation is stated as greater than approximately 10–50 K, whereas only differences below 5 K are declared falsifying; outcomes from 5 K to roughly 10 K are left unresolved.
